title: What not to put on the site for a small clinic
metaTitle: Small clinic website mistakes worth cutting
excerpt: Cut stock smiles and a procedure list from a small clinic site. Keep the room, the clinician, and a clear way to book. A shorter, truer page is easier to trust.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, someone editing a layout down, for an article about what to take off a clinic site.
caption: A hand, a blue pen, and sketches. Cutting the page is part of the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a small clinic remove from its homepage?
faqs.answer: Remove stock smiles, a long procedure list, autoplay video, and slogans about welcome or wellness that do not name the room or the clinician. Keep a true picture, the name of who patients will see, the fee shape or an honest substitute, and a way to book or call. The first screen has room for the decision and little else.

faqs.question: Are patient testimonials a mistake?
faqs.answer: They are a mistake when they promise a medical result, name someone without real permission, or replace the facts about the visit. A process quote, with consent, can live on a proof page. A carousel of unnamed praise on every template is noise. Anxious patients are looking for the room and the rules, not a chorus.

faqs.question: Is a short clinic website less credible?
faqs.answer: No. A short site that shows the room, the clinician, the fee, the access facts, and the booking is more credible than a long one performing taste. Add a page when a real question needs it, such as preparation or referrals. Do not add pages to look established.

markdown:
The small clinic website mistakes that worry an anxious patient are usually things you added. Stock smiles and a procedure list reassure the team that the site looks complete. They confuse someone who is trying to decide whether they can walk in.

Keep the room, the clinician, and a clear way to book a visit. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long one that performs taste.

## Cut the stock smile

The smile from a photo library is the first cut. It is not your room and it is not your clinician. Patients notice the lighting, the teeth, and the feeling that the person does not work where the address says. Once they notice, the hours and the fee are read with suspicion.

Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a page shows first-hand experience, and it gives extra weight to trust on topics that can affect someone's health. A photograph of your own chair is first-hand. A rented grin is the opposite. If you do not have the photo yet, use type and the booking. Do not borrow a face for the gap.

Cut the cousins of that smile. Models in coats. Families in a park you do not own. Handshakes. A child used as a prop. Before-and-after pairs in the hero. Each of these performs care without showing the visit. Performance is what an anxious reader is braced against.

Replace the frame with the entrance, the waiting chairs, or the clinician in the real room. Caption it with a fact. "Two steps. First visits happen in this room." The picture gets to stay when it proves something the sentence also says.

## Cut the procedure list from the door

A menu of every treatment feels diligent. On the homepage it asks a frightened person to self-diagnose before they are allowed to book. They search for the worst word, or they cannot find their word and leave. Neither is the job of the front door.

Move the detail to a services page written as visits. First visit. Follow-up. A question before you book. Each one gets a boundary, including what belongs in urgent care instead of your diary. The homepage keeps three names at most, under the booking, in the patient's language.

Cut synonym pages that exist so each procedure can "have a page." Thin pages with the same smile and a swapped noun are how a small clinic starts to look like a directory. Google's warning about many pages made in the hope that some will rank is the content version of this habit. One honest visit page is stronger than twelve doorways. Redirect the extras so old links do not rot.

Also cut the interactive symptom checker you do not staff. A quiz that implies a diagnosis, then dumps the person into a general inbox, is a clinical tone you do not want. If they are unsure which visit to book, the desk can sort them. Offer the phone. Do not offer a toy.

## Cut the language that performs warmth

"Welcome to our family." "Your wellness journey starts here." "We care more." These lines fill the first screen and say nothing about the hour. A patient in pain does not need to be welcomed into a family of strangers. They need the room, the name, and the fee.

Replace each line with a fact the desk already says.

- Who they will see.
- How long the first visit usually takes.
- Whether a procedure happens that day.
- What the fee covers.
- How to get in, including the steps.
- When the phone is answered.

Warmth is those facts, delivered without a joke at their expense. Chirpy copy about needles or "do not be a baby" should come off every template. It does not make the clinic approachable. It makes the clinic sound like it has not noticed that some readers are scared.

Cut urgency. Countdown timers, "only two slots left" banners, and popups that fire before the room is visible. Unless the diary is actually closed and you explain the waitlist, scarcity is pressure. Pressure is a poor bedside manner. A plain sentence, "We are booking into next month," is allowed because it is operational.

## Cut the trophy case

Award badges, "as seen in," and a row of insurer logos are the visual small talk of clinic templates. They push the booking down the phone screen. A registration a patient can check is not a trophy. Link it from the about page in words. Leave the badge mosaic off the hero.

Testimonials that promise a cure, or that you cannot attribute, belong on the cut list. A consented quote about the process, "they told me about the stairs before I came," can live on a proof page. A carousel of five-star widgets on every page is noise, and the widgets are often slow. Speed matters because the room photo and the button are the page.

Community sponsorships and renovation stories can move to a footer note. They are not why someone with a swollen joint is here. A small clinic does not need to look busier than it is. Busy, on a health site, can read as "they will rush me." Quiet and specific reads as "they have time to explain."

Do not publish headcount, revenue, or a dramatic founding year to seem established. Publish the names. A two-clinician clinic is easier to trust when it looks like two clinicians, not like a hospital campaign.

## Cut motion, widgets, and duplicate doors

Autoplay video, sliders, and chat bubbles that cover "Book a visit" are mistakes even when a vendor calls them engagement. They delay the room and they steal the thumb's target. Hanabi's bar on a marketing site is to be fast before being clever: Next.js, Tailwind, and Motion only when it explains a step. A clinic homepage rarely has a step that needs an animation. The still of the room is the explanation.

Cut a second booking path that does not match the first. Header says "Book." A popup says "Request a callback." The footer says "Enquire." Three verbs, three queues. Pick "Book a visit" and "Call," and make the rest of the site obey. Duplicate doors are how notes go missing.

Cut PDF packs as the way to learn the fee or the preparation. A PDF does not fit a phone, does not get updated when the fee changes, and does not have a booking button. Put the fee and the preparation in HTML. Keep a PDF only when a referrer truly needs a printable sheet, and do not let it be the only copy.

Cut a blog you do not maintain. An abandoned news section dated two years ago makes the clinic look closed. If you write, write about how visits work, in the same voice as the desk, and keep the dates honest. If you do not, remove the nav item. Google's people-first questions include whether the page is maintained or sloppy. A stale post is a sloppy signal on a health site.

## A cut you can finish this week

Open the homepage on a phone. Mark each block. Shows the room. Names the clinician. Books or calls. Anything else is a candidate.

1. Delete the stock hero. Use the room or the face, or type if you must.
2. Remove the procedure grid from the first screen.
3. Replace the welcome headline with the visit and the person.
4. Put the fee shape and the access line where a thumb can reach them.
5. Unstick every widget that covers the button.
6. Read the screen aloud to someone who is not on staff.

If they can say where they would go, who they would see, and how they would book, you have cut enough. If they cannot, you removed a fact. Put the fact back. Do not put the slogan back.

Keep a note of what you removed so the next refresh does not restore the template. On a Hanabi project those notes sit in the client portal with the brand files and the page docs. The public site stays small on purpose. The reason is written down.

## What a short clinic site still includes

Short is not empty. The visit, the person, the fee shape, the hours, the access, the cancellation rule, and the urgent-care boundary are the content. A single scrolling page can hold them if each one is true. A large site that dodges them is the mistake.

Do not cut the accessible name of the booking button, the text alternative on the room photo, or the error text on the form. Those are not decoration. Minimalism here means fewer performances. It means more sentences a patient can use.

Re-read the homepage whenever the diary changes. A new procedure, a departed clinician, a new step at the door. The cut list is a habit. The patient who arrives next month deserves the same plain page as the one who arrived the week you edited it.

If the next site on your desk is a law practice rather than a clinic, the fearful reader changes, and so does the proof. [What the homepage has to prove for a law practice](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-a-law-practice) starts from that different first screen.
